comm.t: King Suratha speaks to the sage Medhas, in his hermitage, having heard that a Goddess called Mahāmāyā both binds and frees (1.54–58). His question (1.60–62) opens the first carita’s story.

mantras.anvaya: भगवन्, यां भवान् महामाया इति (ब्रवीति), सा देवी का हि?
mantras.anvaya_en: A direct question (का हि सा देवी) with a relative clause (यां भवान् … ब्रवीति) whose verb stands at the start of 1.61.
mantras.lit: O blessed one, who indeed is that Goddess whom your honour (calls) ‘Mahāmāyā’ —
mantras.tr: Revered sir, who is this Goddess whom you call Mahāmāyā?
mantras.tr_note: The verb of the relative clause, ब्रवीति, stands at the beginning of 1.61; the readable translation draws it back.

comm.t: The king takes up the name the sage used (1.55–56) and asks who she is. The question is the hinge of the whole text: everything that follows, through chapter 13, is Medhas’s answer.

Suratha’s questions in 1.60–62 — who she is, how she arose, what she does, her power, her nature, her origin — are traditionally read as the plan of the Devī Māhātmya: the three caritas show her arising and her deeds, and the hymns show her nature.

morph.note: √ब्रू inserts ī before consonant-initial strong endings: ब्रव् + ई + ति. Third person because the subject is the honorific भवान् (1.60).
Past participle of उद् + √पद् with the -na affix (पद् + न → पन्न; d + t → tt, ud-panna → utpanna). Used as a finite past: ‘how did she arise?’

mantras.anvaya: (यां भवान् महामाया इति) ब्रवीति। द्विज, सा कथम् उत्पन्ना? अस्याः कर्म च किम्? सा देवी यत्प्रभावा, यत्स्वरूपा, यदुद्भवा च, …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first word completes the relative clause of 1.60. Two direct questions follow (कथम् … किम्), then three indirect questions in compound form, resumed by तत्सर्वम् in 1.62.
mantras.lit: — calls (Mahāmāyā): how did she arise, and what is her deed, O twice-born? And of what power that Goddess is, of what nature, of what origin —
mantras.tr: How did she come to be, O brāhmaṇa, and what are her deeds? What is her power, what her true nature, and from where does she arise?
mantras.tr_note: कर्म is singular (‘deed’); the readable version renders it as the collective ‘deeds’.

comm.t: The king asks six things: how she arose, what she does, her power, her nature, her origin — and, in 1.62, he asks to hear it all. He addresses Medhas as द्विज, a brāhmaṇa.

The sage’s answer (1.64–66) qualifies the first question at once: she is eternal, and is said to ‘arise’ only when she becomes manifest for the gods’ work. The questions about power and nature are answered less by definition than by the stories and the hymns.

morph.note: Infinitive in -tum with guṇa of the root vowel (श्रु → श्रो-तुम्), complement of इच्छामि: ‘I wish to hear’.
The -tas ablative of the pronoun: त्वत्तः ‘from you’ (equivalent to त्वत्), regular with verbs of hearing and learning.

mantras.anvaya: ब्रह्मविदां वर, तत् सर्वं त्वत्तः श्रोतुम् इच्छामि।
mantras.lit: All that I wish to hear from you, O best of the knowers of Brahman.
mantras.tr: All this I long to hear from you, O best of those who know Brahman.

comm.t: The king’s request closes: he wants to hear all of it from the sage, whom he honours as the best of Brahman-knowers. Medhas begins his answer at once (1.63).
A modern reading: the king who has lost his kingdom does not ask for it back here; he asks to understand. The text lets the desire to know come before the desire to regain.

comm.t: Medhas answers King Suratha (with the merchant Samādhi listening) in his hermitage. His answer runs from the Goddess’s eternity (1.64) into the first story, the slaying of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
